title: Tovino Thomas Crashes the College Fest. Athiradi Lands on SonyLIV in Five Languages, and the Diaspora Gets the Whole Joke.
excerpt: The Malayalam action-comedy that turned a banned campus festival into mayhem is now a click away in Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Hindi too. A reformed don who wants to be a singer? Mollywood, never change.
body:
The trailer opens on a college that has buried its own party. Years ago, Aarohan — the kind of campus festival that defines a generation of students — was banned after a night that went catastrophically wrong. Then a civil-engineering kid called Samkutty, played by the impossibly likeable Basil Joseph, decides the fest must live again. What could go wrong? In Malayalam cinema, the answer is always: gloriously, hilariously, everything.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=syBtRf69q6s

Athiradi has arrived on SonyLIV, streaming from June 19 — and crucially for everyone reading this from a flat in Jersey City or a semi in Hounslow, it is available not just in Malayalam but in Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Hindi. That is the kind of multi-language drop that quietly changes the diaspora viewing equation. You no longer have to be a Mollywood loyalist with subtitles half a beat behind the punchlines. You can text the group chat, press play, and everyone is in on it at once.

!Basil Joseph — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

"It is a banger of a Saturday watch — the kind of breezy, sharply timed entertainer that Malayalam cinema produces with maddening ease while the rest of the country chases ₹400-crore spectacle."
https://x.com/cinejosh/status/2067825909059747892

At the centre of the chaos is Tovino Thomas, who continues his run as one of the most watchable leading men working in any Indian language right now. Here he plays Sreekuttan Vellayani, a former goon nursing an unlikely dream: he wants to be a singer. Read that again. A reformed local don with stage ambitions, colliding with a bunch of college kids trying to resurrect their festival. Tovino has the swagger to sell the menace and the lightness to undercut it — that rare actor who can be the threat and the joke in the same frame.

The setup escalates exactly the way you want it to. Samkutty lands a coup by roping in Vineeth Sreenivasan as a guest performer. Then a bruised ego sends everything sideways: Sreekuttan, humiliated during the run-up to the fest, retaliates by kidnapping Vineeth and music director Shaan Rahman. Suddenly a campus event becomes a rescue mission, and a comedy-drama reveals the bigger gang lurking underneath its goofy surface.

!Jersey City — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

"What seemed to be a simple event turned out to be a really chaotic festival." — the premise of Athiradi, in one line

This is Arun Anirudhan's directorial debut, co-written with Paulson Skaria, and it carries the fingerprints of a very particular Malayalam sensibility — the one that lets slapstick and genuine stakes share a room without either feeling cheap. The film first hit cinemas on May 14, 2026 after a paid premiere the night before, did its theatrical lap, and has now been picked up for a second life on streaming. The music is by Vishnu Vijay, with cinematography from Samuel Henry and editing by Chaman Chakko. And in a detail that tells you how much this was a labour of love, Tovino himself co-produced alongside Basil Joseph, Dr. Ananthu S and Sameer Thahir.

There is a meta-pleasure in watching Basil Joseph — himself a director of breakout hits — play the wide-eyed dreamer here, while Tovino vamps it up as the antagonist with a microphone fantasy. Mollywood has always been generous about letting its filmmakers act and its actors produce, and Athiradi is that ecosystem at play. The ensemble fills out with Zarin Shihab and Riya Shibu, and the whole thing moves with the confidence of an industry that knows exactly what its audience came for.

For the diaspora, the calculus is simple. The theatrical window has closed; the trip to a faraway multiplex playing one 9:45 pm Malayalam show on a Tuesday is no longer the only option. Athiradi is now sitting on your home screen, dubbed into the language your cousins actually speak, ready for a weekend that does not require a passport or a designated driver. SonyLIV's regional play keeps getting sharper, and snapping up a crowd-pleaser like this — fresh off its theatrical run — is exactly how you build a streaming habit in a household that grew up on Saturday-night family films.

Is it high art? No, and it is not trying to be. It is a banger of a Saturday watch — the kind of breezy, sharply timed entertainer that Malayalam cinema produces with maddening ease while the rest of the country chases ₹400-crore spectacle. Press play, let Tovino's would-be singer terrorise a college fest, and remember that sometimes the best night in is a movie that just wants to make you laugh. The festival is back on. So is your weekend.
